# `silk/mem/pointer`

<!-- Generated by silk doc-reference. Do not edit by hand. -->

Raw data pointers: make them, check them for null, move along them, and read and write through
them.

## When to use
Use raw pointers at foreign function boundaries and in storage that native code owns. Inside
Silk code, use references (`&T`, `&mut T`) and slices (`&[T]`). The compiler checks those, but
it does not check raw pointers.

## Details
The pointer types are:

- `*const T` and `*mut T`: one element, never null.
- `[*]const T` and `[*]mut T`: many elements, never null. The pointer has no length.
- `?*const T`, `?[*]mut T`, and so on: the same types, but null is allowed.
- `*const align(1) T`: a pointer that is not aligned for `T`. Use [`Pointer.readUnaligned`](#Pointer.impl.readUnaligned) and
  [`Pointer.writeUnaligned`](#Pointer.impl.writeUnaligned) with it.

A pointer is `Copy`. It does not own its target, it does not borrow it, and it does not keep it
alive. Making, comparing, and converting pointers is safe. Reading and writing through a pointer
is `unsafe`.

## Gotchas
A pointer that is not null can still point to memory that was released or that is not
initialized. Each `unsafe` operation lists what the caller must prove. If the caller is wrong,
the behavior is undefined.

## Examples
### Write and read through pointers to a local value and a slice
```silk
import silk.core.option { Option }
import silk.mem.pointer { Pointer }

fn third(values: &[i32]) -> i32 {
  return match move Pointer.nonNullMany<i32>(Pointer.fromSlice<i32>(values)) {
    Option<[*]const i32>.Some { value: first } => unsafe Pointer.read<i32>(
      unsafe Pointer.at<i32>(first, 2)
    )
    Option<[*]const i32>.None => 0
  }
}

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  let mut value: i32 = 1
  let target = Pointer.fromMutRef<i32>(&mut value)
  unsafe {
    Pointer.write<i32>(target, 12)
  }
  let values = [10, 20, 30]
  if value + third(&values) != 42 {
    return 1
  }
  return 0
}
```

Import as `Pointer` with `import silk.mem.pointer { Pointer }`.

<a id="Pointer.impl.bytes"></a>

### Associated function `bytes`

```silk
pub unsafe fn bytes<T>(pointer: ?*const T) -> ?[*]const u8
```

Returns `pointer` as a pointer to bytes. It does not read memory.

#### When to use

Use `bytes` to read the first fields of a foreign record whose full size is not known, without
reading the whole `T`.

#### Gotchas

The result is null if `pointer` is null. It has no length and does not keep the memory alive.
Each byte that you read through it must be readable and initialized.

<a id="Pointer.impl.address"></a>

### Associated function `address`

```silk
pub fn address<T>(pointer: ?*const T) -> usize
```

Returns the address of `pointer` as a number. Null gives 0.

#### Details

It does not read memory. The result has the pointer width of the target. You cannot make a
pointer from the result.

<a id="Pointer.impl.fromRef"></a>

### Associated function `fromRef`

```silk
pub fn fromRef<T>(value: &T) -> *const T
```

Returns a pointer to the value that `value` refers to.

#### Gotchas

The borrow ends when this call returns. The pointer does not keep the value alive or prevent
other access to it. Each later use must make sure that the value is still alive.

<a id="Pointer.impl.fromSlice"></a>

### Associated function `fromSlice`

```silk
pub fn fromSlice<T>(values: &[T]) -> ?[*]const T
```

Returns a pointer to the first element of `values`.

#### Gotchas

The pointer has no length. Pass `values.length` to the code that uses it. The result type
allows null, so use [`Pointer.nonNullMany`](#Pointer.impl.nonNullMany) before you index it. The pointer does not keep the
slice alive.

<a id="Pointer.impl.read"></a>

### Associated function `read`

```silk
pub unsafe fn read<T: Copy>(pointer: *const T) -> T
```

Returns a copy of the `T` at `pointer`. The pointer must be aligned for `T`.

#### Gotchas

The caller must prove that `pointer` points to a live, readable, initialized `T`. For storage
that is not aligned, use [`Pointer.readUnaligned`](#Pointer.impl.readUnaligned).

<a id="Pointer.impl.write"></a>

### Associated function `write`

```silk
pub unsafe fn write<T: Copy>(pointer: *mut T, value: T) -> ()
```

Writes `value` to the `T` at `pointer`. The pointer must be aligned for `T`.

#### Gotchas

The caller must prove that `pointer` points to live, writable storage for a `T`. For a `T`
that is not `Copy`, use [`Pointer.put`](#Pointer.impl.put).

<a id="Pointer.impl.take"></a>

### Associated function `take`

```silk
pub unsafe fn take<T>(pointer: *mut T) -> T
```

Moves the `T` out of the storage at `pointer` and returns it.

#### Details

`T` does not need to be `Copy`. After the call, the caller owns the value and the storage is
uninitialized. Fill it again with [`Pointer.put`](#Pointer.impl.put), or do not read it again.

#### Gotchas

The caller must prove that `pointer` points to a live, initialized `T` that no other code will
take or drop. Otherwise the value is dropped two times.

<a id="Pointer.impl.dropInPlace"></a>

### Associated function `dropInPlace`

```silk
pub unsafe fn dropInPlace<T>(pointer: *mut T) -> ()
```

Drops the `T` at `pointer` in place and leaves the storage uninitialized.

#### When to use

Use `dropInPlace` to destroy a value whose storage is released next, such as a heap cell. It
runs the drop on the pointee directly. `drop Pointer.take(pointer)` copies the value out first.

#### Gotchas

The caller must prove that `pointer` points to a live, initialized `T` that no other code will
take or drop. Otherwise the value is dropped two times.

<a id="Pointer.impl.put"></a>

### Associated function `put`

```silk
pub unsafe fn put<T>(pointer: *mut T, value: T) -> ()
```

Moves `value` into the storage at `pointer`. It does not drop the value that was there.

#### Details

`T` does not need to be `Copy`. The storage owns `value` after the call.

#### Gotchas

The caller must prove that `pointer` points to live, writable storage for a `T`. If the
storage holds an initialized value, that value is not dropped and leaks.

<a id="Pointer.impl.borrow"></a>

### Associated function `borrow`

```silk
pub unsafe fn borrow<'a, A, T>(anchor: &'a A, pointer: *const T) -> &'a T
```

Returns a shared reference to the `T` at `pointer` that lives as long as the borrow of
`anchor`.

#### When to use

Use it in a handle type that owns storage through a pointer. The handle passes itself as
`anchor`, so the reference cannot outlive the handle. `Arc.get` works this way.

#### Gotchas

The caller must prove that `pointer` points to an initialized `T` that stays valid while
`anchor` is borrowed, and that no code changes it during that time, except through atomic
operations.

<a id="Pointer.impl.borrowMut"></a>

### Associated function `borrowMut`

```silk
pub unsafe fn borrowMut<'a, A, T>(anchor: &'a mut A, pointer: *mut T) -> &'a mut T
```

Returns an exclusive reference to the `T` at `pointer` that lives as long as the exclusive
borrow of `anchor`.

#### When to use

Use it in a guard type. The guard passes itself as `anchor`, so the reference cannot outlive
the guard. `MutexGuard.get` works this way.

#### Gotchas

The caller must prove that `pointer` points to an initialized `T` that stays valid while
`anchor` is borrowed, and that no other code reads or writes it during that time.

<a id="Pointer.impl.borrowMany"></a>

### Associated function `borrowMany`

```silk
pub unsafe fn borrowMany<'a, A, T>(anchor: &'a A, pointer: [*]const T, length: usize) -> &'a [T]
```

Returns a shared slice of the `length` elements that start at `pointer`. The slice lives as
long as the borrow of `anchor`.

#### When to use

Use it in a handle type that keeps elements in storage it reaches through a pointer, such as
bytes stored inline after a header. The handle passes itself as `anchor`, so the slice cannot
outlive the handle.

#### Details

`anchor` only sets the lifetime of the result. It is not read. The call does not check the
pointer or the length, so the result costs the same as a slice that you already have.

#### Gotchas

The caller must prove all of these:

- `pointer` points to `length` initialized `T` values, one after another in one allocation.
  The pointer must be aligned for `T`, also when `length` is 0.
- `length` times the size of `T` fits in `isize`.
- The values stay valid while `anchor` is borrowed, and no code changes them during that
  time, except through atomic operations.

#### Examples

```silk
import silk.core.option { Option }
import silk.mem.pointer { Pointer }

struct Inline {
  bytes: [u8; 4],
}

fn view<'a>(cell: &'a Inline) -> &'a [u8] {
  let first = match move Pointer.nonNullMany<u8>(Pointer.fromSlice<u8>(&cell.bytes)) {
    Option<[*]const u8>.Some { value } => value
    Option<[*]const u8>.None => Intrinsic.trap("an array is never at null")
  }
  unsafe { return Pointer.borrowMany<Inline, u8>(cell, first, 3) }
}

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  let cell = Inline { bytes: [1, 2, 3, 4] }
  let bytes = view(&cell)
  if bytes.length != 3 || bytes[2] != 3 {
    return 1
  }
  return 0
}
```

<a id="Pointer.impl.borrowManyMut"></a>

### Associated function `borrowManyMut`

```silk
pub unsafe fn borrowManyMut<'a, A, T>(anchor: &'a mut A, pointer: [*]mut T, length: usize) -> &'a mut [T]
```

Returns an exclusive slice of the `length` elements that start at `pointer`. The slice lives
as long as the exclusive borrow of `anchor`.

#### When to use

Use it in a handle or guard type that keeps elements in storage it reaches through a pointer.
The handle passes itself as `anchor`, so the slice cannot outlive the handle, and nothing else
can use the handle while the slice lives.

#### Details

`anchor` only sets the lifetime of the result. It is not read. The call does not check the
pointer or the length, so the result costs the same as a slice that you already have.

#### Gotchas

The caller must prove all of these:

- `pointer` points to `length` initialized `T` values, one after another in one allocation.
  The pointer must be aligned for `T`, also when `length` is 0.
- `length` times the size of `T` fits in `isize`.
- The values stay valid while `anchor` is borrowed, and no other code reads or writes them
  during that time.
